title: Line charts: trend, scale and dual axes (and why to avoid them)

videos.script: Here are two lines on one chart. Horta's orders in the Southeast, and in the North. {{two}} The North line starts low, climbs fast, and crosses the Southeast in the middle of last year. It looks like the North has caught up. {{cross}} It has not. The Southeast still sells more than five times as much. {{truth}} The chart has two vertical axes, one on each side, and each line is drawn against its own. Whoever made the chart chose both ranges. And with those two choices, they chose where the lines cross. {{axes}} Line charts are the best tool we have for showing change over time. A line joins the months in order, and the eye reads its slope as speed. {{slope}} But the slope depends on the frame. On the axis range. On the shape of the box. On a second axis nobody asked for. {{frame}} This lesson is about drawing lines whose slopes are honest, and about the alternatives to a dual axis. {{plan}}
